evidence.text: A man 人 with outstretched arms
Pictograph of a person with outstretched arms, representing the meaning "big".
天大，地大，人亦大。故大象人形。古文大(他達切)也。凡大之屬皆从大。

Characters in the same phonetic series (大) (Zhengzhang, 2003)
Pictogram (象形): a person facing forward. Original form of 夫 (OC *pa, *ba, “man”), phonetically borrowed for 大 (OC *daːds, *daːds, “big”). Compare 人, which represents the profile of a person.
Often explained as an ideogram of a person with outstretched arms; however, the ancient scripts do not show stretching.
Compare with 尢, which is a man with bent legs. Compare also 立, similar to 大, and 交, in which the legs are crossed. Compare also 文, which is a man with arms outstretched and a crest or tattoo on his chest, and to 夭, which is a man with arms outstretched and leaning to side (running or marching vigorously).
See the top component of 泰 in the original version (𡙌), the top component of 赤 and the bottom component of 奐 (well visible in some fonts). Related to 太.
Unrelated to 买, in which the bottom component is the stylization of a cowrie.
Cognate with 太 (OC *tʰaːds, “too, excessively”), 泰 (OC *tʰaːds, “big”). Wang (1982) also lists 誕 (OC *l'aːnʔ, “big, magniloquent, ridiculous”) as a cognate, which Schuessler (2007) suggests is cognate with 延 (OC *lan, *lans, “to extend”) instead. There are no unambiguous Tibeto-Burman cognates. Proto-Tibeto-Burman *taj (“big”), from which came Written Tibetan མཐེ་བོ (mthe bo, “thumb”), Anong tʰɛ (“big, large, great”), Mikir tʰè, ketʰè (“big, large, great”), Burmese တယ် (tai, “very”), is often compared with. There is no final –s in the Tibeto-Burman words, but a –y, which, according to James Matisoff, “indicates emergent quality in stative verbs”. Also compare Chinese 多 (OC *ʔl'aːl, “many, much”), 都 (OC *taː, “all”).
天大，地大，人亦大。故大象人形。古文大(他達切)也。凡大之屬皆从大。

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Multi-function Chinese Character Database), CUHK
evidence.text: The database analyzes 大 as a front-facing standing adult, with arms hanging down. It gives the original sense as ‘adult’ in contrast with child and derives ‘big’ from that contrast. It reports bronze-inscription 大 meaning ‘big’, opposite 小, citing the Lü Zhong (郘鐘) inscription ‘大鐘八聿(肆)’. It also says early 大 and 夫 were one graph with both adult-male and large senses; 夫 later differentiated by adding a short stroke, which most scholars regard as decorative. This supports adult-human imagery but not the popular outstretched-arms explanation.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 漢字甲骨部件分析：大

evidence.field: 大 entry and Duan Yucai commentary
evidence.text: The Eastern Han dictionary entry glosses 大 through the comparison ‘Heaven is great, Earth is great, and humans are great too,’ and says the graph depicts a human figure. It records 大 as the ancient form of 亣; Duan Yucai comments that 大 and 亣 were one character with slightly different shapes, assigned to separate sections in later dictionary organization. This is an early historical explanation, not independent proof of the graph's prehistoric origin.
evidence.title: 說文解字「大」

evidence.text: The article, citing Herrlee G. Creel, describes the ancient graph 大 as a human figure specifically denoting an adult, distinguished from the more general 人 graph. It regards this as consistent with the graph structure and quotes the Shuowen account. This is corroborative scholarly discussion, not a dated primary occurrence of 大.

editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

gaps: No individual 大 oracle-bone specimen was retrieved or visually inspected. The Academia Sinica database page was opened, but its search interface did not yield a character-specific record here.

The dossier’s outstretched-arms story conflicts with the opened CUHK specialist account, which describes arms hanging down; no inspected glyph image settles details directly. Treat the adult-human reading as a source analysis, not direct visual verification in this session.

The exact earliest dated attestation of 大 used for ‘adult’ or ‘big’ was not established. The CUHK source cites a bronze inscription with the ‘big’ sense, but the inscription transcription page attempt failed and a reliable date for that specific vessel was not confirmed.

Graphic development can be stated only generally as continuity through oracle-bone, bronze, small-seal, and standard forms. Specific graphic changes, possible scribal corruption, and variant chronology were not demonstrated by the opened sources.

The adult-to-big semantic link is explicitly proposed by the specialist dictionary, but an independently dated chain of intermediate semantic uses was not collected. The Shuowen explanation is historical evidence for a traditional account, not confirmation of prehistoric formation.

No sound component or whole-graph phonetic loan is proposed for 大 in the supported analysis. Accordingly, there is no depicted object name to reconstruct or sound match to validate. Other senses and uses—including 大 used for 太-like readings—are usage/word-history matters and should not be mistaken for graphic derivation.

Modern reading evidence from the inspected specialist pages is Mandarin dà and Cantonese daai6. Search results report historical forms, but one key dictionary page was inaccessible; different Old Chinese reconstructions are system-specific and should not be collapsed into a single pronunciation history.

The CText dictionary page returned 403 Forbidden when opened, and the Zhonghuashu inscription transcription attempt returned 502 Bad Gateway. Their attempts are recorded; no claims depending solely on their unopened page contents are treated as inspected evidence.

No component decomposition applies to standalone 大; the supported analysis treats the whole graph as an adult human pictograph. No sound component or whole-graph phonetic loan is proposed, so no component or object-name pronunciation comparison is needed.

The outstretched-arms explanation in local excerpts conflicts with the inspected CUHK description of arms hanging down. The education resource also describes a standing person but does not detail limb positions. No image pixels were inspected in this research stage.
No precisely dated earliest 大 oracle-bone specimen or dated use for ‘adult’ was established. CUHK cites a bronze inscription for ‘big’ but its exact vessel/date was not verified in this session.

The proposed adult-to-big semantic development is an explicit dictionary analysis; an independently dated sequence of intermediate senses was not collected. The 夫 relationship and the claim that its added stroke is decorative are source assertions, not a dated character-by-character derivation demonstrated here.

The broad oracle-bone-to-bronze-to-small-seal-to-standard sequence is supported as a sequence of labels, but detailed stroke changes, a specific corruption event, and chronology of variants remain unestablished.

No individual oracle-bone specimen was retrieved for pixel inspection. The Commons file description identifies a Sinica source image, but its original image retrieval failed in the web tool.

No exact earliest dated attestation of 大 for ‘adult’ or ‘big’ was established. CUHK cites a bronze inscription for ‘big’, but the cited vessel’s date and inscription were not independently verified here.

No sound component or whole-graph phonetic loan is proposed for standalone 大; no source-word/object-name reconstruction is relevant to this analysis.

The scanned 字源 page confirms the printed 大 headword and the relevant prose, but the book's cited historical glyph specimens are reproduced as forms with bibliographic pointers; this research did not independently inspect those cited source volumes or artifacts.

The book edition is 李學勤主編《字源》, 天津古籍出版社 / 遼寧人民出版社, 2012, ISBN 9787552800692. The publisher/catalogue URL supplied here is a WorldCat search endpoint rather than an inspected item record; page evidence is the directly inspected supplied scan, PDF p. 922, printed p. 907.
The arms-extended description in 字源 conflicts with CUHK's arms-hanging-down analysis. No need to resolve this anatomical detail to support the broader interpretation as a frontal human figure.
Neither the scanned book nor the inspected online specialist sources establish a dated chain of attestations demonstrating the proposed semantic development from ‘adult’ to ‘big’.
CUHK cites the bronze phrase 郘鐘「大鐘八聿(肆)」 for ‘big’, but the vessel's date and inscription were not independently verified from a primary inscription record here.
The source scan's broad historical form sequence does not by itself establish precise stroke-by-stroke changes or any scribal corruption.
The official Unicode Unihan lookup for U+5927 failed to open; the local HSK1 row for Mandarin dà is not external click-through evidence.

字源 PDF p. 923 is the supplied OCR continuation for the 大 entry, but its original scan was not attached or inspected in this invocation; claims relying on continuation-only text remain unverified against pixels.

字源 PDF p. 922, printed p. 907: the book describes 大 as a frontal person with hands spread; CUHK describes arms hanging down. The inspected Sinica record supports a frontal human figure but does not settle arm position.

No independently dated chain establishes that ‘adult’ preceded and developed into ‘big’. The accounts inspected present this as an analysis; neither their citation of the 郘鐘 phrase nor lists of later senses alone prove the semantic chronology.
The exact date and primary inscription reading for CUHK’s cited 郘鐘 example were not independently checked here.

The bibliography URL for 字源 is a WorldCat search endpoint, not an inspected catalogue record. The scan’s printed page number 907 and page contents were directly inspected; edition metadata comes from the supplied source packet.

items.period: Shang period style; the page identifies the script style, not a securely dated specimen in the SVG itself
items.caption: This modern redraw in Shang oracle-bone style shows 大 as a frontal figure with a long central body, arms extending sideways, and separated legs. The human-figure reading is supported, though accounts differ on the arms’ position.
items.alt: Black glyph with a long upright body, two sideways arms, and separated legs.
items.selection_reason: It gives a useful early-style example of the whole-graph human-figure analysis. The arms’ position remains disputed.
items.rights: CC0 1.0 / public domain as stated on the Commons file page.

items.period: Early Western Zhou specimen is cited as a source; file depicts Western Zhou bronze-script style
items.caption: This modern redraw in Western Zhou bronze-script style shows a frontal figure with a tall central body, broad sideways arms, and legs below. It illustrates the script style; it does not identify a particular inscription or date a use of 大 for “big.”
items.alt: Black glyph with a tall central body, broad sideways arms, and two curved legs.
items.selection_reason: It adds a distinct bronze-script-style example. The redraw is not the inscription cited for the meaning “big.”
items.rights: Commons states the file is available under CC0 and separately lists Richard Sears permission/copyright information; verify terms at source before reuse.

items.period: Shuowen seal-script style; the digital file is a modern redraw
items.tradition: Seal script as represented in Shuowen-style reference forms
items.caption: This modern redraw in Shuowen seal-script style has a central upright, outward-sloping arms, and two long legs. It shows a dictionary-script form without establishing a precise path of graphic change from earlier forms.
items.alt: Black seal-style glyph with a central upright, sloping arms, and two long legs.
items.selection_reason: It provides a later script-style comparison; the evidence supports broad form comparison, not a precise sequence of changes.
items.rights: CC0 1.0 / public domain as stated on the Commons file page.

limitations.text: These modern redrawings show named script styles, not photographs of ancient objects. Accounts describe the human figure’s arms differently, and the glyphs alone cannot establish its original meaning or settle that disagreement.

The examples allow broad comparison across script styles, but do not establish a precise chronology of graphic changes or date the earliest use of 大. The proposed development from “adult” to “big” lacks a documented dated sequence of intermediate uses.
